strengths: Addresses a core bottleneck in offline GFlowNet training: eliminating the reliance on vulnerable proxy reward models and avoiding crude constraint penalties on unobserved transitions.

The conceptual framework is well-motivated: leveraging inverse reinforcement learning on reward-rebalanced offline trajectories to extract edge rewards, and using them indirectly (via DAG pruning and prioritized backward sampling) to prevent error propagation into policy gradient updates.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across synthetic (Hypergrid with varying sizes and noise/suboptimality levels) and structured scientific domains (anti-microbial peptide design and sEH molecule design).

Strong empirical results: TD-GFN achieves notable sample efficiency, rapid convergence, and maintains mode diversity, even outperforming oracle/proxy-based baselines with significantly fewer training trajectories.

Thorough appendix containing ablation studies (rebalancing, pruning vs. backward sampling), sensitivity analyses (pruning threshold K), runtime/memory comparisons, and compatibility tests with different GFN objectives (FM, TB) and offline RL objectives.
weaknesses: Clarity on DAG pruning implementation in open-ended combinatorial spaces: In Section 3.2 and Algorithm 1, the text describes pruning edges and removing disconnected components globally from the environment DAG. While this is feasible for finite grids (Hypergrid), combinatorial spaces like Molecule Design have astronomical state spaces where global DAG materialization and global connectivity checks are impossible. The exact implementation details for how pruning and reachability are enforced during online backward/forward rollouts in molecular environments should be clarified in the main text.

Dependence on adversarial IRL: Extracting edge rewards via GAIL introduces min-max adversarial optimization as a preliminary phase. Adversarial training can be sensitive to hyperparameters and optimization dynamics, potentially adding tuning overhead compared to non-adversarial offline objectives.

Impact of pruning on target distribution fidelity: Pruning edges fundamentally alters the reachable support of the GFlowNet, meaning the resulting policy cannot sample from the original full state space support. While beneficial for focusing on high-reward modes, a formal discussion or quantification of the trade-off between mode coverage/L1 error on the full space vs. pruned subgraphs under different pruning thresholds would strengthen the theoretical grounding.

strengths: Compelling motivation: The paper tackles a central bottleneck in offline GFlowNet training—namely, the susceptibility of proxy reward models to out-of-distribution inaccuracies and gradient corruption—by proposing a proxy-free framework.

Principled integration with IRL: Formulating the transition-level credit assignment via maximum causal entropy IRL and leveraging the theoretical bridge between entropy-regularized RL and GFlowNets is conceptually sound and well-grounded.

Extensive empirical evaluation: The method is validated across diverse benchmarks, including Hypergrid, Anti-Microbial Peptide (AMP) sequence design, and fragment-based molecule design. The comparisons against diverse baselines (COFlowNet, offline RL like CQL/IQL, and proxy-based GFNs) are comprehensive.

Thorough appendix analysis: The supplementary material includes detailed ablation studies, sensitivity analyses over the pruning threshold K, evaluations under extreme data scarcity (down to 30 trajectories), and comparisons across different objectives (TB vs. FM vs. CQL).
weaknesses: Ambiguity and scalability issues in DAG pruning: Section 3.2 and Algorithm 1 specify pruning the environment DAG G = (V, E) based on edge rewards and subsequently removing all edges disconnected from the root node s0. In combinatorial domains like Biosequence and Molecule Design, the state space and DAG are astronomical in size (e.g., > 10^50 states), making pre-pruning or global graph connectivity traversals computationally intractable. Although Section D.5 briefly mentions predicting pruned edges via neural network forward passes, the exact implementation of local vs. global pruning and reachability enforcement in large state spaces remains underspecified.

Reliance on complete trajectory data: Unlike standard proxy-based methods that only require terminal state-reward pairs (x, R(x)), TD-GFN critically depends on full offline trajectories. As highlighted in Appendix E, training quality drops substantially when trajectories are generated via uniform or heuristic backward sampling. This limits the applicability of TD-GFN in real-world offline settings where only static end-products and measured rewards are cataloged (e.g., historical chemical or protein databases).

Restricted support for backward training: In Phase 3, trajectories are sampled exclusively backward from the terminal states present in the offline dataset. While the policy can generalize structurally through neural function approximation at test time, the model is never trained on terminal reward feedback outside the support of the dataset, which may limit out-of-distribution discovery when the dataset has low mode coverage.

Computational overhead and instability of adversarial IRL: Phase 1 relies on GAIL-style adversarial training to recover edge rewards, which introduces min-max optimization instability and additional hyperparameters (discriminator learning rate, actor learning rate) that need careful tuning for each domain.

strengths: Compelling and well-motivated framework: The paper introduces TD-GFN, an innovative proxy-free offline GFlowNet method that leverages inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) to extract dense edge-level utility scores from rebalanced offline trajectories.

Robust indirect guidance design: By utilizing the learned edge rewards solely for DAG pruning and prioritized backward trajectory sampling—while keeping policy gradient updates grounded entirely on empirical terminal rewards—the method neatly avoids error propagation and proxy exploitation that plague standard reward proxy models.

Strong and comprehensive empirical evaluation: Across synthetic (Hypergrid), semi-realistic (AMP sequence design), and realistic benchmarks (molecule generation), TD-GFN demonstrates consistent improvements over strong baselines (including COFlowNet, offline RL algorithms like CQL/IQL, and proxy-based GFNs) in both convergence speed and discovered mode diversity.

Extensive robustness and ablation studies: The authors thoroughly investigate data scarcity (down to 30 trajectories), varying data quality (expert, mixed, median, inverted reward), pruning threshold sensitivity, and modular ablations across multiple training objectives (TB, FM, CQL).
weaknesses: Practicality and scaling of DAG pruning in large action/state spaces: In combinatorially vast domains (such as molecule fragment assembly or sequence generation), the full environment DAG cannot be explicitly enumerated or globally pruned. While the authors mention evaluating edge validity via forward passes during sampling, the operational mechanics and computational overhead of pruning dynamic graphs vs. static tabular DAGs should be formalized and detailed in the main text.

Strong assumption on full trajectory availability: TD-GFN fundamentally relies on complete, high-quality trajectories rather than just offline state-reward pairs $(x, R(x))$. In many real-world chemical or biological discovery settings, only final candidates and assay values are available. As shown in Appendix E (Figure 18), performance drops considerably when intermediate trajectories are generated via naive heuristics.

Sensitivity and training complexity of adversarial IRL: Incorporating GAIL into the preprocessing pipeline introduces adversarial minimax optimization with associated hyperparameters (learning rates $\alpha, \beta$, discriminator iterations, and the pruning threshold $K$), potentially complicating tuning on novel tasks compared to simpler offline objectives.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: training Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) purely from offline trajectory data without relying on noisy or out-of-distribution proxy reward models.

Principled and innovative methodology: grounding the transition importance via maximum causal entropy Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) and using the distilled edge rewards strictly for structural DAG pruning and prioritized backward sampling, which prevents proxy fitting error propagation during gradient updates.

Solid theoretical foundations: provides rigorous theoretical characterizations (Theorems 3.1, 3.2, and extensive proofs in Appendix B) demonstrating the unique recovery of the backward policy under canonical gauges, perturbation bounds, and mode-survival guarantees under estimation noise.

Extensive and convincing empirical validation: evaluated across diverse domains including synthetic Hypergrids (up to $20^4$ and $256^2$), biological sequence design (AMPs), fragment-based molecular generation, and listwise recommendation (MovieLens 1M).

Thorough comparisons and ablation studies: includes strong baselines across offline GFlowNets (COFlowNet), offline RL (CQL, IQL, BraVE), and imitation learning (BC, GAIL); thoroughly investigates the role of dataset rebalancing, pruning strategies, backward sampling, objective compatibility (FM, TB, SubTB, DB), and computational efficiency.
weaknesses: Multi-stage pipeline and adversarial complexity: TD-GFN relies on an initial adversarial IRL/GAIL phase, which introduces minimax optimization instabilities and additional training hyperparameters prior to GFlowNet training.

Scalability of global DAG pruning: while the paper demonstrates applicability on molecular and slate recommendation tasks, implementing hard pruning over very large or continuous/unconstrained combinatorial action spaces can become challenging unless edges are filtered on-the-fly via neural evaluations.

Degeneracy in tree-structured DAGs: as noted by the authors in Appendix D.2, in environments with unique backward trajectories (trees, e.g., left-to-right sequence generation), prioritized backward sampling degenerates to terminal state sampling, leaving DAG pruning as the primary active mechanism.

strengths: Principled and well-motivated conceptual framework: The paper establishes a sound connection between maximum causal entropy IRL and offline GFlowNet training via the entropy-regularized RL equivalence (Tiapkin et al., 2024). Distilling offline trajectories into dense transition-level edge rewards provides a structured way to guide policy learning without relying on an error-prone global proxy reward model.

Robust architectural design against error propagation: By utilizing learned edge rewards strictly for DAG pruning and prioritized backward trajectory sampling—while keeping gradient updates anchored solely to ground-truth dataset terminal rewards—the method cleverly avoids the out-of-distribution value estimation errors that commonly plague reward proxy models and offline RL value functions.

Solid theoretical underpinning: Appendix B provides a comprehensive theoretical analysis, proving that terminal reweighting preserves the canonical backward policy, characterizing the IRL edge reward as the log conditional incoming flow score, providing TV perturbation bounds for the recovered backward policy, and establishing path-bottleneck survival guarantees and total variation distortion bounds under DAG pruning.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Experiments span synthetic benchmarks (Hypergrid at various scales and data regimes: Expert, Mixed, Median, Bad, and extreme data scarcity), biosequence design (AMP), molecular optimization (sEH), and recommendation slates (ML-1M). Across these tasks, TD-GFN consistently demonstrates faster convergence, better target distribution fitting, and superior candidate quality/diversity compared to both proxy-based and proxy-free baselines (e.g., COFlowNet, CQL, IQL, BraVE).
weaknesses: Practicality and scaling of DAG pruning in massive or open-ended action spaces: Pruning requires scoring edges across the environment DAG. While tractable for moderate action spaces and gridworlds, for domains with vast or continuous action branching (e.g., full combinatorial molecular graphs with extensive fragment libraries or long-horizon tasks), evaluating and pruning edges globally can become computationally demanding or require non-trivial approximations.

Degeneration on tree-structured state spaces: In environments with strictly tree-structured transitions (such as left-to-right biosequence generation where each state has a unique parent), prioritized backward sampling degenerates to sampling terminal states directly from the dataset. While the authors acknowledge this in Appendix D.2, it implies that the core backward sampling mechanism contributes less in tree-like MDPs compared to general DAGs.

Sensitivity and heuristics for pruning hyperparameter $K$: Although Appendix E.5 provides sensitivity curves, selecting $K$ in practice relies on an empirical heuristic (maximizing the ratio of retained recorded transitions over random transitions), which may be challenging to calibrate reliably on unfamiliar or uncurated real-world offline datasets.

Reliance on adversarial IRL training: Adversarial imitation learning (GAIL-style min-max optimization) can be notoriously unstable or sensitive to optimization hyperparameters (learning rates $\alpha, \beta$), potentially adding training complexity compared to direct supervised regression or non-adversarial offline objectives.

strengths: Principled and novel offline framework: By connecting GFlowNet training to entropy-regularized RL, the paper cleverly leverages inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) to extract transition-level edge rewards, addressing both the out-of-distribution reward exploitation of proxy-based methods and the over-conservatism of existing proxy-free methods.

Robust decoupling of guidance and policy optimization: Using learned edge rewards strictly for DAG pruning and prioritized backward sampling—while restricting gradient updates to ground-truth terminal rewards—effectively shields policy optimization from function approximation errors in the IRL phase.

Rigorous theoretical foundation: Appendix B establishes solid theoretical guarantees, including the invariance of the backward policy under trajectory reweighting (Proposition B.1), unique recovery under the parent-normalization gauge (Theorem B.5), perturbation bounds in total variation (Theorem B.7), and robust mode survival under bounded estimation error (Theorem B.9 and B.11).

Thorough empirical evaluation across diverse domains: The method is validated on synthetic hypergrids (including extreme data scarcity and large scales), biosequence design (AMP), molecular graph generation (sEH), and recommendation slates (MovieLens 1M), consistently outperforming prior proxy-free methods (COFlowNet), proxy-based GFNs, and discrete offline RL baselines (CQL, IQL, BraVE).

Extensive ablations and analysis: The appendix provides thoughtful sensitivity analyses (e.g., pruning threshold K), wall-clock and memory profiling, ablations on backward sampling and rebalancing, visual inspections of learned edge rewards, and compatibility tests with different GFN objectives (FM, TB, SubTB, DB).
weaknesses: Pruning scalability and heuristic thresholding: While pruning is shown to work well on discrete DAGs, evaluating and filtering transitions can be computationally challenging in environments with very high branching factors or continuous actions. Additionally, the selection heuristic for the threshold hyperparameter K relies on an empirical ratio of retained transitions, which may require careful tuning in new domains.

Sensitivity and training complexity of adversarial IRL: Learning edge rewards via GAIL introduces adversarial minimax optimization, which is notoriously sensitive to training stability and hyperparameters, particularly on very sparse or noisy offline datasets.

Requirement of trajectory-level data: Unlike proxy reward approaches that only require terminal state-reward pairs (x, R(x)), TD-GFN depends on the presence of intermediate trajectory transitions in the offline dataset, limiting direct applicability when only final designs are recorded.
